title: Kinetic & gravitational PE
examples: How do I calculate the energy when something is moving?
What is the difference between kinetic and potential energy?
Can you show me an example of energy changing from one form to another?

explain.say: Today we learn about two types of energy. We will look at kinetic energy first. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. It depends on how much mass something has and how fast it moves.
The formula for kinetic energy is one half times mass times velocity squared. Remember that mass is measured in kilograms. Velocity is measured in meters per second.
Next we look at gravitational potential energy. This energy is stored due to height. It depends on mass, the acceleration due to gravity, and the height. The formula is mgh.
The formula for gravitational potential energy is mass times gravity times height. Gravity near Earth is approximately nine point eight meters per second squared. Height is measured in meters.
Energy can change from one form to another. This is energy conversion. For example, a stretched spring stores potential energy. When released, it converts to kinetic energy.
In real life, a roller coaster converts energy. At the top, it has maximum potential energy. As it goes down, this changes to kinetic energy. At the bottom, it is fastest.

faq.q: Does the mass have to stay the same when energy converts?
faq.a: Yes, the mass of the object generally stays the same during energy conversion. You can also say that the object's mass does not change. Another way to ask is, 'Is mass constant during energy change?'
asks: Does mass change when energy changes?
Is mass conserved in these calculations?

faq.q: Do I need to use the value for gravity every time?
faq.a: Yes, unless told otherwise, use the standard value for gravity, which is nine point eight meters per second squared. You might also ask, 'What is the value for g?'
asks: What is the standard value for g?

faq.q: If I use the conservation of energy, what do I set equal to what?
faq.a: You set the initial total energy equal to the final total energy. This means PE plus KE at the start equals PE plus KE at the end. You could also ask, 'How do I use energy conservation?'
asks: What is the energy at the top equal to?
How do I set up the energy equation?

faq.q: What if the object is moving at a constant speed?
faq.a: If the speed is constant, the kinetic energy is constant, and there is no change in energy due to motion. You could also ask, 'Is KE zero if it's not moving?'
asks: What is the KE if v is zero?
Does KE change if speed is constant?

faq.q: Is the formula for kinetic energy always half times mass times velocity squared?
faq.a: Yes, for classical mechanics problems, the formula is consistently one half times mass times velocity squared. You could also ask, 'Is there another way to write KE?'
asks: What is the correct KE formula?
Can I skip the one half in the KE formula?

facts: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed.
Gravitational potential energy depends on height.
The standard value for gravity near Earth is nine point eight meters per second squared.
Total mechanical energy is the sum of KE and GPE.

quiz.say: A 2 kilogram object is dropped from a height of 10 meters. What is its total energy at the bottom?
quiz.why: At the bottom, the height is zero, so GPE is zero. The total energy equals the initial GPE: 2 times 9.8 times 10, which is 196 Joules. If we use 10 for g, it is 200 Joules.

wrong.1: This only calculates the potential energy using the height, forgetting the mass.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates KE using only the height value.
wrong.3: This incorrectly calculates KE using only the mass and height.

quiz.say: A 5 kilogram object moves at 4 meters per second. What is its kinetic energy?
quiz.why: You use the kinetic energy formula: one half times 5 times 4 squared, which is one half times 5 times 16, equaling 40 Joules.

wrong.0: This incorrectly squares the mass instead of the velocity.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates one half times mass times velocity.
wrong.3: This incorrectly calculates mass times velocity squared.

quiz.say: A ball is held at a height of 5 meters. If its mass is 3 kilograms, what is its potential energy?
quiz.why: You use the GPE formula: 3 times 9.8 times 5, which equals 147 Joules. This shows the stored energy.

wrong.1: This incorrectly multiplies mass by height only.
wrong.2: This incorrectly calculates mass times gravity only.
wrong.3: This incorrectly calculates mass times gravity only, ignoring the height.
